seoTitle: Agitation in the ED: De-escalation, IM Meds, Withdrawal
metaDescription: The agitated patient in the ED: medical checks first, de-escalation, IM olanzapine, haloperidol or lorazepam by cause, restraint rules, CIWA-Ar and COWS.
h1: Agitation, withdrawal and psychiatric emergencies: the ED pathway
dek: For the student on an EM or psychiatry rotation when a patient is shouting in triage and a resident asks what is next. The medical checks that come first, de-escalation, which IM drug fits which cause, restraint rules, alcohol and opioid withdrawal, and the suicide screen.

shortAnswer.text: Vital signs with temperature, oxygen and a fingerstick glucose before any psychiatric label; new agitation is presumed medical until proven otherwise.
One clinician, at least 2 arm's lengths away, in short sentences; offer oral medicine with the patient choosing the agent and route. Verbal de-escalation often works in under 5 minutes.

shortAnswer.lead: Match the IM drug to the cause.
shortAnswer.text: Psychosis: an antipsychotic, such as olanzapine 10 mg IM or haloperidol 5 mg IM with lorazepam 2 mg IM (guidelines differ on the first choice). Drunk: haloperidol if medication is unavoidable, no benzodiazepine. No psychosis, or withdrawal: lorazepam 2 mg IM. IM olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine is not recommended.
Supine rather than prone, constant observation, a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour, a 4-hour order in adults, and off as soon as the danger has passed.
Symptom-triggered in hospital, diazepam first line, lorazepam if the liver is impaired. After a withdrawal seizure, lorazepam 2 mg IV, never phenytoin.

shortAnswer.lead: Thiamine with glucose, not instead of it.
shortAnswer.text: High-dose IV thiamine for suspected Wernicke, before or with any glucose, but a low glucose is never held back for it.

COWS 12 or more, not sedated, and at least 12 hours after a short-acting opioid or 24 after methadone (TIP 63; the label allows 4 hours after a short-acting opioid with clear moderate withdrawal), then 2 to 4 mg under the tongue, repeated about 2 hours later if needed.
The ASQ's four questions, then thoughts of suicide right now if any is yes. An acute positive stays in sight for a STAT mental health evaluation.

sections.heading: What do you do first with an agitated patient in the ED?
sections.intro: A safe room, enough staff, and vital signs with temperature, oxygen and a fingerstick glucose. A high temperature with a fast pulse on a drug or in withdrawal gets cooling, fluids and an IV benzodiazepine.

sections.heading: Which findings decide the route: medical, toxic, withdrawal or psychiatric?
sections.intro: Vital signs and the first look separate a medical emergency, a hot patient and plain agitation. If de-escalation fails, psychosis, alcohol or delirium picks the drug.

sections.heading: Which drug for which agitated patient, and how is withdrawal treated?
sections.intro: An antipsychotic for psychosis, haloperidol rather than a benzodiazepine on top of alcohol, a benzodiazepine when there is no psychosis or there is withdrawal, and restraint only when less restrictive measures fail.

sections.heading: How do you assess withdrawal, psychosis and suicide risk?
sections.intro: CIWA-Ar for alcohol, COWS and the last opioid for opioid withdrawal, vitals, exam and cognition before calling psychosis primary, and the ASQ asked directly.

sections.heading: When does the patient go home, get admitted or need a hold?
sections.intro: Imminent suicide risk with refusal of care means an involuntary hold under local law. Mild withdrawal without risk factors can go home with a support person, and buprenorphine started in the ED goes home with follow-up within 72 hours.

checklist.heading: After an IM dose or restraint: what to monitor

items.text: Constant observation with vital signs while restrained; check oxygen and glucose at once if they could not be obtained before the restraint.
Face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour of starting restraint or seclusion (CMS).
Order length: 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, 1 hour under 9; a new order to continue.
Supine where possible, nothing pressing on the chest, neck or abdomen; manual holding not routinely beyond 10 minutes.

After rapid tranquilization: pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and consciousness at least hourly; every 15 minutes if sedated, after alcohol or drugs, or with a physical illness.
Before a repeat IM olanzapine: check for orthostatic hypotension, and no repeat sooner than 2 hours after the first dose.
Alcohol withdrawal: CIWA-Ar every 1 to 2 hours in hospital; delirium, or over 40 mg of diazepam needed in an hour, means ICU-level care.

rounds.present: Give the medical screen first, then the route you took, so your resident hears why you chose the drug. One-liner: 47-year-old man in alcohol withdrawal, last drink 30 hours ago, with a withdrawal seizure 2 years ago, who struck out at a nurse in triage. Glucose 112, no injury and no rigidity, so no medical emergency at the door. One calm voice did not work and he refused oral medicine; with no hallucinations or delusions and not drunk, he took the benzodiazepine route, lorazepam IM, and calmed. CIWA-Ar 18 with a past seizure makes him moderate to severe and high risk: admitted to a monitored bed on symptom-triggered benzodiazepine by CIWA-Ar, diazepam first line since his liver tests are near normal, with thiamine, and magnesium, phosphate and potassium replaced as needed. At 4 hours his CIWA-Ar is 9 and his pulse 96. Watching for escalation: delirium, or over 40 mg of diazepam needed in an hour, means ICU-level care.

pimp.q: Why not a benzodiazepine for the violent drunk patient?
pimp.a: Benzodiazepines compound the respiratory depression of alcohol. When medication is unavoidable, an antipsychotic is preferred, haloperidol having the longest record with minimal effect on breathing.

pimp.q: Why not give IM olanzapine with IM lorazepam?
pimp.a: Together they cause excessive sedation and cardiorespiratory depression, so IM olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine is not recommended.

pimp.q: Why is phenytoin wrong after an alcohol withdrawal seizure?
pimp.a: NICE does not offer it, and anticonvulsants did no better than placebo for withdrawal seizures in a Cochrane review. A single 2 mg dose of IV lorazepam cut recurrence within 6 hours from 24.4% to 3% in an ED trial.

pimp.q: Why can't buprenorphine go in as soon as the patient asks for it?
pimp.a: It is a partial agonist with strong receptor affinity that can displace a full agonist and precipitate withdrawal, so the first dose waits for objective withdrawal: a COWS of 12 or more, at least 12 hours after a short-acting opioid and at least 24 hours after methadone (TIP 63).

pimp.q: How do you tell akathisia from worsening psychosis?
pimp.a: Akathisia is inner restlessness with a drive to move, usually within the first 2 weeks of an antipsychotic or a dose increase. More antipsychotic is wrong: lower the dose or switch, add propranolol or a benzodiazepine, and ask about suicidal thoughts.

pimp.q: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity and confusion days after haloperidol. What do you stop?
pimp.a: Every dopamine blocker. Atypical agents cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome too, so switching keeps the trigger going. Then ICU, aggressive cooling, fluids and electrolyte correction; anticholinergics treat dystonia, not this.

traps.text: A urine drug screen before the exam. It seldom changes the ED disposition; the history and examination find most medical illness.
Restraints before talking. Unless the patient is actively violent, restraint does not come before de-escalation.
A benzodiazepine on top of alcohol intoxication. It compounds respiratory depression; haloperidol is the choice when medication is unavoidable.
Haloperidol alone for delirium tremens. A benzodiazepine is the treatment, with phenobarbital as rescue, and antipsychotic monotherapy raises the risk of complicated withdrawal.
Clonidine or a beta blocker to treat withdrawal. They mask the signs and prevent neither seizures nor delirium tremens.

IV dextrose first, thiamine once the bloods return, in a confused drinker with nystagmus. Thiamine goes in before or with glucose at treatment doses, never delaying treatment of a low glucose, and brain imaging cannot exclude Wernicke.
Flumazenil in benzodiazepine withdrawal. It risks refractory seizures and arrhythmias; restart a benzodiazepine and taper slowly.
Not asking about suicide directly, or letting a risk scale decide who goes home. Ask the ASQ questions; screening never replaces the clinical assessment.

faq.q: What is the first-line medication for an agitated patient in the ED?
faq.a: It depends on the cause, and oral medicine comes first if the patient will take it. For psychosis, an antipsychotic such as olanzapine 10 mg IM, or haloperidol 5 mg IM with lorazepam 2 mg IM. In alcohol intoxication, haloperidol without a benzodiazepine. With no psychosis, or in withdrawal or stimulant intoxication, a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam 2 mg IM. Guidelines differ on the preferred IM regimen.

faq.q: How do you treat alcohol withdrawal in the ED?
faq.a: Score it with CIWA-Ar in an awake, alert patient and ask about past seizures or delirium tremens. Mild withdrawal without risk factors can be treated as an outpatient with a support person. Moderate to severe or high-risk withdrawal gets symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing in a monitored bed, diazepam first line or lorazepam with liver impairment, plus thiamine and electrolyte replacement; sources differ on admitting moderate withdrawal without risk factors.

StatPearls grades 8 or less as mild, 8 to 15 as moderate and over 15 as severe, so its bands meet at 8. This pathway treats a score of 8 or more, or a past seizure or delirium tremens, age over 65, illness, benzodiazepine use or no support, as moderate to severe or high risk, with symptom-triggered dosing in a monitored bed; sources differ on admitting moderate withdrawal without risk factors. It is valid only in an awake, alert patient.

faq.q: When can you start buprenorphine in the ED?
faq.a: Once withdrawal is objective and the patient is not sedated or intoxicated: a COWS of 12 or more, at least 12 hours after a short-acting opioid and at least 24 hours after methadone (TIP 63). The label allows 4 hours after a short-acting opioid with clear moderate withdrawal. Start 2 to 4 mg under the tongue and repeat about 2 hours later if needed, typically up to 8 mg on day 1.

faq.q: How long can a patient stay in restraints?
faq.a: Only until the danger has passed. A face-to-face evaluation is due within 1 hour (CMS), and Joint Commission orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17 and 1 hour under 9, with a new order to continue. The patient is held supine, watched constantly and given medication to calm them; restraint beyond 4 hours raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis.

faq.q: What do you do with a positive suicide screen in the ED?
faq.a: It depends on the acuity question. Thoughts of killing themselves right now is an acute positive: keep the patient in sight, remove dangerous objects and get a STAT mental health evaluation; they cannot leave until evaluated. A non-acute positive gets a brief safety assessment of plan, means, past attempts and supports. A positive screen alone does not justify involuntary care.
